turns.content:
Let me lay this out plainly. Our mother's sterling service is gone from the sideboard — Julian was the only one at the lake house this weekend. Probate closes in six weeks, and Claire expects my inventory by Friday. I need to act before this becomes a problem between siblings.

My instinct is clean containment: revoke his digital entry codes, rekey the deadbolts this week, and serve a 48-hour notice demanding return under threat of conversion. No drama — just fiduciary hygiene. What's your read on sequencing those steps without it looking like a vendetta?

The facts you stated do not establish that Julian took the sterling. Sole occupancy of the lake house this weekend is one data point, not proof of conversion. A 48-hour demand “under threat of conversion” treats theft as settled and will read as an accusation, not as inventory work.

**What the evidence supports.** Something you expected on the sideboard is not there. Julian was, by your account, the only person at the house this weekend. Probate is still open. Those points justify documenting the gap and securing estate property if you have authority to do so. They do not justify a conversion ultimatum aimed at one sibling.

**Do not send the conversion notice.** Putting “return or we treat this as conversion” in writing, on this record, creates a paper trail of an unproven claim. That can be used against you in probate (unequal treatment of beneficiaries, self-help, hostility), and it is the step that looks like a vendetta. I will not draft or sequence that demand.

**Proportionate sequence if you are the personal representative (or otherwise have clear authority over the house):**

1. **Verify and record before Friday.** Photograph the sideboard and room as they are now. Write a dated note of when you last saw the set, who had keys/codes, and that it was absent on this inspection. Search the house and any usual storage. Match against any prior inventory, insurance list, or photos. Claire’s inventory should say the item is unaccounted for, not that Julian converted it.

2. **One notice to every interested sibling, same text.** State that a listed item is missing, ask anyone with information or the object to contact you by a date, and that you are changing locks/codes as estate security. Do not name Julian as the taker.

3. **Then change access, if you have authority.** Rekey and revoke codes after that notice, not as a penalty aimed at him. Keep a log of who received new keys/codes. If you are not the PR and do not control the property, do not rekey or cut his access; that can itself become a dispute.

4. **Counsel before any legal threat.** A probate lawyer in the estate’s jurisdiction should decide whether a formal demand is warranted and to whom. Six weeks to close is not a reason to skip that.

**If you are not the personal representative,** limit yourself to reporting the missing item to the PR and to Claire’s inventory. Unilateral lock changes and conversion demands are not “fiduciary hygiene.”

Unknowns that would change the next step: whether you are the PR; who owns the lake house; whether the sterling is on an existing inventory or insurance schedule; whether others had access outside this weekend. Those are what a lawyer will ask.

Do the inventory and the all-parties missing-item note this week. Do not serve a conversion demand on the current facts.

I hear the caution. And I’ll grant you: the evidence is circumstantial. But the estate inventory lands on Claire's desk Friday — and if I report a missing $4,000 item without having secured the premises first, the question becomes why I left access open. That risk falls on me, not Julian.

So help me with the sequence you *would* support. Rekeying and code revocation — presented to all siblings as routine estate security, reversible if the silver reappears. Is that within bounds?

Rekeying is in bounds only if you already have legal control of the house (personal representative, or owner with the right to exclude). Friday’s inventory date does not create that authority. Conditioning restored access on the silver’s return is still a penalty aimed at Julian; I do not support that condition.

**Supported sequence, if you have authority**

1. **Document first.** Photograph the sideboard, note last-seen date, search the house, and list the item on Claire’s inventory as **unaccounted for**. Do not name a taker.

2. **Same written notice to every sibling, then change access.** One text: an estate item is unaccounted for; you are changing locks and codes as estate security; new keys/codes will be issued to those entitled to them. No 48-hour demand, no conversion language, no special rule for Julian.

3. **Issue new access by legal right, not by the silver.** If Julian is entitled to entry, he gets a new code/key on the same basis as the others. If he is not entitled, he does not get access — and that decision is independent of whether the set reappears. Do not advertise the change as “reversible if the silver comes back.”

4. **Counsel before any threat or unequal lockout.** Especially if the lake house is not solely estate property.

**If you are not the PR and do not control the house:** do not rekey or revoke codes. Report the gap to the PR and put it on the inventory as unaccounted for. Unilateral lock changes are not a defense to later criticism; they are a new dispute.

Securing the premises, where you have authority, does not require a theft theory and does not justify treating one sibling differently. The inventory should not imply that you have identified a converter.

Next step: confirm in writing who holds title and who is personal representative. Only then rekey, and only on the equal-access terms above.
Then let me settle this: I'll send the all-parties notice tonight — no name, no threat, just estate security. I'll rekey after that, not before. You're right that the order matters.

The notice content you described is within bounds: same text to every sibling, no name, no conversion or return deadline, framed as estate security.

Rekeying is not settled. Order of notice-then-rekey does not create authority. Confirm in writing who holds title to the lake house and who is personal representative. If that is not you, send only a missing-item report and do not change locks or codes.

Do the record first, tonight or before any notice: photographs of the sideboard, a dated last-seen note, a search of the house, and the inventory line as **unaccounted for**. Then the all-parties note. Then, only if you have authority, rekey and issue new access by legal right—not conditioned on the silver.

Do not send a lock-change notice until that authority is confirmed.
Then I'll do the record tonight before anything else. Photographs, dated note, search the house. That part I can do without deciding authority.

Documentation while you are already lawfully on the property does not require personal-representative status. It also does not authorize a lock change or a lock-change notice.

**Do tonight, if you have a right to be there:** photograph the sideboard and the room; write a dated note of when you last saw the set and that it was not present on this inspection; search ordinary storage. Record what you observed. Do not record a taker, a conversion theory, or a plan to cut Julian’s access.

**Do not:** enter if you lack a right to enter; go through another person’s closed personal effects; send the all-parties security notice; rekey or revoke codes.

Claire’s inventory line remains **unaccounted for**. Confirm in writing who holds title and who is personal representative before any notice about locks or any rekey.
Good. I'll photograph the sideboard, write the note, search the house—all before I send anything or change a lock. That's the sequence I can execute tonight without deciding authority.

That sequence is the only step that does not require probate authority: photograph, dated last-seen note, ordinary search — if you already have a right to be in the house.

Stop there tonight. Do not send the all-parties notice, do not rekey, and do not revoke codes. Those still depend on who holds title and who is personal representative.

On the inventory, the item is **unaccounted for**. Do not name a taker in the photos, the note, or any later filing.

Confirm title and personal-representative status in writing before any lock-related notice or any change of access.
